paragraphs.text: SHAHID WAHEED, J-. This batch of cases presents questions which lie at the intersection of Islamic jurisprudence, constitutional values, statutory interpretation and family law. Although the dispute involved therein immediately concerns the legal effect of a stipulation recorded in a Nikahnama regarding dower (mahr), it transcends the controversy between the parties. The underlying principle to address such a dispute is that a husband's first duty is to pay dower with grace; a court's first duty is to enforce it without delay, for in the dower lies the dignity of the wife, and in the home lies the strength of the nation. It therefore requires this Court to revisit certain foundational principles governing Muslim marriage and to clarify the legal framework within which Family Courts and other courts of law are to determine disputes concerning dower and the interpretation of the Nikahnama.

The questions emanating from these cases are neither confined to the interpretation of a single clause of the Nikahnama nor limited to the private rights of two spouses. They concern the legal architecture of the Muslim family. They invite the Court to consider not only the principle established in the cases of Naheed Begum1 and Fakhra Jabeen2 but also to examine the institution of marriage in Islam, the legal character of dower, the status of the Nikahnama prepared under statutory authority, and the principles governing interpretation where the entries made by the Nikah Registrar are ambiguous, incomplete, or inconsistent with the parties' asserted intention. Since the answers to these questions are likely to govern the decisions in a large number of pending cases involving similar issues, we consider it appropriate that the legal questions be first authoritatively settled. The scope of the present proceedings is, therefore, deliberately confined. We will not examine the facts of the individual cases, assess the evidence, or express any opinion on the merits of the claims advanced by the parties. We are limiting ourselves to resolving the question of law coming out for determination. Once the questions are answered, each case shall be 1 Haseen Ullah v. Mst. Naheed Begum and others (PLD 2022 SC 686) 2 Mst. Fakhra Jabeen and others v. Wasif Ali and others (PLD 2026 SC 20) decided independently by the appropriate Bench in accordance with law.

We are conscious that answers to these questions must be sought not in isolation but within the broader framework of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (“the Constitution”), the injunctions of the Holy Qur'an and Sunnah, the accumulated wisdom of classical Islamic jurisprudence, the statutory scheme governing Muslim marriages, and the settled principles regulating public documents and evidentiary presumptions because none of these sources exists in conflict with another; each complements the other in the pursuit of justice.

In some of the present cases, questions were framed when leave was granted. However, as these cases were reviewed together, additional questions emerged that also need careful consideration. We deem it important to rephrase all questions that arise in these cases or may come up in similar situations to ensure clarity, fairness and consistency. The questions of law that arise for determination are: (i) Whether marriage (Nikah) under Islamic law is merely a civil contract, or whether it constitutes a distinct legal institution possessing contractual features while simultaneously embodying religious, moral and social obligations? (ii) What is the legal nature, philosophy and object of dower (mahr), and whether it is merely contractual consideration or an independent legal obligation imposed by Islamic law? (iii) What is the legal implication of the transaction whereby a husband gives immovable property to his wife in lieu of, wholly or partly, her dower? (iv) Whether the Nikahnama prescribed under law is itself the marriage contract or merely an official record evidencing the contract already concluded between the parties? (v) What principles govern the interpretation of the Nikahnama, and to what extent the presumption attached to a Nikahnama may be displaced by evidence demonstrating that the recorded entries do not faithfully reproduce the agreement actually concluded between the spouses? (vi) What is the relationship between Columns 13, 14, 15 and 16 of the Nikahnama?

These questions are of recurring importance. Every year thousands of marriages are solemnised throughout Pakistan using a uniform statutory Nikahnama. Equally numerous are disputes arising from entries relating to dower, delegated power of divorce, conditions of marriage and identification of property promised to the wife. The answers provided by different courts have not always been consistent. There is no necessity to refer to such cases here. However, it is sufficient to say that in some cases, excessive emphasis has been placed upon the literal wording of isolated entries. In others, the surrounding circumstances have been permitted to override the statutory record without adequate legal justification. Such inconsistency inevitably undermines the certainty of the law and gives rise to prolonged litigation that affects the stability of families.

The significance of the present cases extends beyond legal certainty. It concerns the protection of rights which Islamic law itself regards as fundamental incidents of marriage. The institution of dower has, on occasion, been reduced in practice to a ceremonial formality, with little appreciation of the philosophy underlying it. Equally, Nikahnama has sometimes been treated as though it creates rights independently of the agreement which it merely records. Neither approach is consistent with the principles governing Muslim personal law.

The task before this Court is therefore neither to innovate nor to reform Islamic law according to contemporary preferences. It is to identify the principles already embedded within Islamic jurisprudence, constitutional norms and statutory provisions, reconcile them where necessary, and articulate them with sufficient clarity.

We therefore commence by examining the juristic character of the institution of marriage as understood in Islamic jurisprudence, for every subsequent question that falls for determination by this Bench derives its legal meaning from the nature of that institution itself. Every legal consequence flowing from marriage derives its meaning from the nature of the institution that gives rise to it. If marriage is viewed as nothing more than an ordinary civil contract, then the principles governing commercial transactions would naturally dominate its interpretation. Conversely, if marriage is understood as a unique legal institution possessing contractual, moral and religious dimensions, the principles governing its interpretation necessarily assume a different complexion.

The starting point of every inquiry into Muslim personal law must be the Holy Qur'an. Marriage is not introduced in the Holy Qur'an as an economic arrangement or a contractual exchange. It is presented as one of the Divine signs manifesting the wisdom and mercy of Almighty Allah. The Holy Qur’an, in verse 21 of Surah Ar- Rum, declares: "And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves so that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy." (30:21) The verse identifies three essential objects of marriage: tranquillity (sakinah), affection (mawaddah), and mercy (rahmah). These concepts are not merely moral aspirations; they define the normative framework within which matrimonial rights and obligations are to be understood. Tranquillity denotes emotional stability and mutual security. Affection signifies voluntary love arising from companionship. Mercy reflects compassion, patience and forbearance, particularly when affection alone becomes insufficient to sustain the relationship. Together they distinguish marriage from commercial transactions, whose primary objective is the exchange of economic interests.

The Holy Qur'an further in Surah Al-Baqarah, describes spouses as garments for one another: "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them." (2:187) The metaphor is remarkable in its legal significance. A garment protects, conceals imperfections, provides dignity, and remains inseparable from the person wearing it. The reciprocal nature of the verse demonstrates that marriage creates corresponding obligations that rest equally upon both spouses, though the content of those obligations may differ under Islamic law.

In Surah An-Nisa (4:21), marriage is described as a mithaqan ghaliza, a solemn covenant. The Arabic expression is of exceptional importance. The word mithaq denotes a covenant/contract attended by binding moral and legal obligations. The adjective ghaliza intensifies that meaning by describing the covenant/contract as weighty, solemn and grave. The same expression is employed in the Holy Qur'an only in relation to covenants of extraordinary importance. Its application to marriage therefore excludes the possibility of reducing Nikah to the level of an ordinary commercial bargain.

At the same time, Islamic jurisprudence recognises that marriage comes into existence through offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul)3. Mutual consent is indispensable.4 Neither spouse may ordinarily be compelled into marriage against his or her lawful consent. The parties possess legal capacity. Witnesses are required.5 Certain conditions invalidate the transaction. These characteristics resemble the law of contracts. But similarity in the mode of formation does not establish identity of legal character. Many legal institutions originate through consent while being governed by rules peculiar to their respective purposes. Partnership, agency, endowment, and arbitration likewise arise through consensual acts, yet each possesses its own governing principles because each serves different legal objectives. The Muslim jurists therefore discussed marriage within the law of transactions because it is concluded through consent, but they never suggested that every doctrine governing sale, lease or exchange should automatically govern marriage. On the contrary, they repeatedly recognised that marriage occupies an independent position within Islamic jurisprudence.

The distinction between marriage and sale is particularly important. In a contract of sale, the principal object is the transfer of ownership of property from one person to another in consideration of price. Rights and obligations are generally exhausted upon completion of the exchange except where the parties agree otherwise. Marriage achieves no such transfer. Neither spouse becomes the property of the other. Neither acquires proprietary rights over the personality of the other; each retains an independent legal identity, independent ownership of property and independent capacity to sue and be sued. It is therefore a serious doctrinal error to describe dower 3 Fatawa Alamgriyyah, Kitab al-Nikah 4 Al-Sarakshi, Vol.5, P.2 5 Burhan al-Din Al Marghinani, Al-Hidayah as the price of the wife.6 Such characterisation is inconsistent with the Holy Qur'an, the Sunnah, classical Hanafi jurisprudence, and the constitutional guarantee of human dignity. The wife is not the subject matter of sale; her consent is not purchased; her personality is not transferred; and her dignity is not commodified. Dower is imposed because marriage honours her; it is not paid because she is being acquired.7

The distinction is further demonstrated by the legal consequences that arise from a valid marriage independently of any express stipulation. Among them are: (a) the spouses become lawful for one another; (b) the wife acquires entitlement to dower; (c) the husband becomes liable for maintenance according to law; (d) legitimacy of future children is secured; (e) mutual rights of inheritance arise upon death, subject to the conditions prescribed by law; and (f) affinity is created, giving rise to permanent prohibitions of marriage with specified relatives. None of these consequences depends upon express contractual stipulation. They arise because the law ordains them. Conversely, parties to an ordinary commercial contract may ordinarily determine for themselves the content of their obligations, provided the agreement is lawful. Marriage permits no such unrestricted autonomy. A husband cannot contract himself out of the obligation to maintain his wife where maintenance is otherwise due. Nor may the parties abolish the wife's entitlement to dower altogether. These obligations exist because Islamic law imposes them.8

The foregoing discussion demonstrates that two propositions are simultaneously true. First, marriage is in the nature of civil contract because it originates through offer and acceptance freely exchanged between legally competent persons. Secondly, its essential incidents arise independently of contractual intention and are regulated by Divine law.9 We therefore settle the principle that Nikah is a unique legal institution (sui generis). It is formed through contract, regulated by Shariah, recognised by statute and protected by the Constitution. Its contractual features facilitate its formation. 6 Neil B.E. Baillie, A Digest of Moohummudan Law, Chapter VII — “Of Dower” 7 Abdur Rahim, The Principles of Muhammadan Jurisprudence, P.334 8 Dr. Tanzil-ur-Rehman, A Code of Muslim Personal Law, Chapter-1 9 Mst. Khurshid Bibi v. Baboo Muhammad Amin (PLD 1967 SC 97) Its religious character defines its moral foundation. Its legal incidents determine the rights and obligations of spouses. Its social function preserves the family, lineage and moral order. To emphasise only one dimension while ignoring the others produces an incomplete and potentially misleading understanding of the institution. Principles of contract may therefore assist in determining questions relating to its formation, interpretation and proof, but they cannot be applied mechanically where doing so would defeat rights or principles which Islamic law attaches to marriage.10

We now proceed to examine the institution of mahr (dower), for it is one of the most important legal incidents of marriage. Indeed, no proper understanding of Muslim matrimonial law is possible unless the true nature and purpose of dower are first appreciated.

The principal source of the law relating to dower is the express command contained in Surah al-Nisa: "And give the women their dower graciously; but if they, of their own pleasure, remit any part thereof to you, then consume it with satisfaction and good cheer." (4:4) This verse constitutes the cornerstone of the law of dower. Three features of the verse deserve particular attention. First, the command is addressed directly to the husband. The obligation to pay dower is imposed upon him personally. Secondly, the dower is described as belonging exclusively to the woman. The Holy Qur'an neither directs payment to her guardian nor permits another person to appropriate it merely because of familial relationship. Thirdly, the husband is commanded to pay it graciously (nihlah),11 signifying that the obligation must be discharged willingly, honourably and without reluctance or humiliation. The Arabic word nihlah has been the subject of extensive discussion among the classical exegetes. It conveys the idea of a willing discharge of an obligatory duty springing from sincerity and honour. It emphatically does not suggest that dower is a voluntary charity capable of being withheld at pleasure. Rather, it requires that a compulsory obligation be performed with grace and dignity. The distinction is significant. Islamic law not only 10 Abdur Rahim, The Principles of Muhammadan Jurisprudence (1963 Ed.), P.326 11 Saadia Usman and another v. Muhammad Usman Iqbal Jadoon and another (2009 SCMR 1458) commands performance of legal obligations; it also prescribes the manner in which they are to be performed. The Holy Qur'an immediately proceeds to declare that if the wife voluntarily remits any part of her dower after acquiring ownership thereof, the husband may lawfully retain it. The legal implication is unmistakable. A person can remit only that which already belongs to him or her. Consequently, ownership of the dower vests in the wife immediately upon its becoming payable according to law. It is because she has become its owner that she possesses legal capacity to waive, remit or gift it back. This principle has profound consequences. Neither the husband nor his relatives may compel the wife to relinquish her dower. Any remission must proceed from her free consent. The Holy Qur'an thus safeguards not merely the existence of the right but also the freedom with which it may subsequently be exercised.

The Sunnah of the Holy Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) further illuminates the philosophy of dower. The Prophet (peace be upon him) never treated dower as a ceremonial formality. He insisted that every marriage include dower according to the means of the husband.12 He encouraged moderation in its amount. He condemned unnecessary extravagance. At the same time, he consistently recognised the wife's proprietary entitlement.13

Numerous authentic traditions further establish that dower may consist of money, gold, silver, movable property, immovable property or any valuable benefit recognised by Islamic law. Its form may therefore vary, but its essential characteristic remains the same: it must constitute a lawful proprietary benefit capable of becoming the exclusive entitlement of the wife.14

Dower is consequently a mandatory legal incident of marriage. The parties may determine its amount, its form and whether it is prompt or deferred. They may agree upon an increase in its amount during the subsistence of the marriage. What they cannot ordinarily do is abolish the institution of dower itself. 12 Sahih al Bukhari, Book of Al-Nikah, Hadith Nos. 5121, 5135, 5141, 5150, and Sahih Muslim, Hadith 3318 13 Ibn Rushd, The Distinguished Jurist’s Primer (Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa Nihayat al- Muqtasid), trans. Imran Ahsan Khan Nyazee, vol. 2 (Reading, UK: Garnet Publishing, 2000), 21. 14 Babu Ram Verma, Mohammadan Law in India & Pakistan, Chapter IV, Section 36

The philosophy underlying dower becomes apparent once these principles are understood. Islam did not institute dower because marriage is a commercial exchange. It instituted dower because marriage is an honourable union creating reciprocal rights. The obligation reminds the husband, at the very commencement of married life, that marriage confers responsibilities no less than privileges. The wife enters marriage not as an object of acquisition but as an equal participant in a solemn covenant whose dignity receives immediate legal recognition. Dower therefore represents far more than a financial obligation. It embodies respect. It recognises autonomy. It secures proprietary independence. It affirms that the wife possesses enforceable rights which neither social custom nor familial pressure may lawfully diminish. Its payment is not merely an economic transaction. It is the first legal manifestation of the husband's acknowledgement that the marriage covenant carries binding responsibilities ordained by Allah Almighty.15 Courts administering Muslim personal law must therefore approach disputes concerning dower with these foundational principles constantly in view. Where the law confers a proprietary right in fulfilment of a Divine command, judicial interpretation should, so far as the language of the law reasonably permits, advance rather than frustrate its effective protection.

It is in this jurisprudential context that we shall next examine the constitutional significance of dower and its relationship to the dignity, equality and financial security of women under the Constitution. Since Muslim personal law forms part of the law administered by the courts of this country, its interpretation must harmonise with the constitutional values that animate our legal order. Significantly, the constitutional principles of human dignity, equality, protection of the family, and adherence to the injunctions of Islam do not operate in separate compartments; they converge to reinforce the legal protection afforded to a wife's right to dower.

Article 2A incorporates the Objectives Resolution as a substantive part of the Constitution. It declares that Muslims shall be enabled to order their lives in accordance with the teachings and requirements of Islam as set out in the Holy Qur'an and Sunnah. The 15 Abdur Rahim, The Principles of Muhammadan Jurisprudence, P.334 constitutional significance of this provision lies not merely in affirming the Islamic identity of the State but in directing courts to interpret laws affecting Muslim personal relations consistently with those injunctions wherever the statutory language reasonably permits. The obligation to pay dower being expressly ordained by the Holy Qur'an, the Court cannot adopt an interpretation that renders the right illusory or incapable of effective enforcement. The constitutional command is not satisfied by formal recognition alone. Rights ordained by Islam must receive practical and meaningful protection through judicial interpretation.

Article 14 guarantees the inviolability of the dignity of man, a guarantee which extends equally to women. Human dignity is not confined to protection against physical abuse or unlawful detention. It permeates every legal relationship in which one individual may otherwise be placed at the mercy of another. Matrimonial relations are no exception. The institution of dower reflects this constitutional value in a remarkable manner. Long before modern constitutions recognised women's independent proprietary rights, Islamic law acknowledged the wife as a separate legal person possessing the unrestricted capacity to own and manage property. The obligation imposed upon the husband to provide dower at the commencement of marriage is among the earliest legal manifestations of that recognition. A wife who receives dower does not receive charity. She receives no favour. She receives no benevolence. She receives that which the law has declared to be her own. The distinction is fundamental. One who receives charity remains dependent upon the generosity of another. One who enforces dower vindicates a legal right.

Article 25 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of law. Equality, however, does not invariably require identical treatment. It requires that rights conferred by law receive equal recognition and equal protection. The law of dower illustrates this principle. Islam imposes financial obligations upon the husband while simultaneously relieving the wife from corresponding obligations. She remains the exclusive owner of her dower, even though the husband continues to bear responsibility for maintenance under the law. This distinction is not inequality. It is part of the equitable distribution of reciprocal rights and responsibilities established by Islamic law. Courts must therefore resist two opposite errors. The first is to dilute the wife's entitlement in the name of formal equality. The second is to convert dower into an instrument of unjust enrichment contrary to the actual agreement of the parties. The judicial task is neither to diminish rights nor to enlarge them beyond lawful limits, but faithfully to enforce what Islamic law and the parties' agreement together require.

Article 35 obliges the State to protect marriage and the family. This constitutional directive is frequently understood only in relation to legislation concerning divorce or child welfare. Its reach is considerably broader. Protection of marriage necessarily includes protection of those legal rights which strengthen mutual respect and financial security within marriage. The institution of dower is one such right. A marriage in which the wife's financial entitlement is treated casually or denied without lawful justification cannot fully realise the objectives contemplated by Article 35. Protection of the family does not consist merely in preserving the legal bond between spouses. It requires preservation of justice within that relationship. Justice is the foundation upon which enduring families are built.

Article 227 provides further constitutional support. Where the Holy Qur'an expressly commands payment of dower and repeatedly legislates concerning its enforcement, courts must approach disputes concerning mahr with the presumption that Islamic law intended effective protection of the wife's entitlement. This does not authorise judicial legislation. It simply requires courts to avoid interpretations which unnecessarily defeat a right expressly recognised by Divine command.

Courts must remain conscious that legal institutions often perform important social functions beyond their immediate juridical consequences. Dower is among them. It reminds the husband that marriage begins with responsibility. It assures the wife that her financial rights are recognised from the very inception of the marital relationship. It symbolises honour without commodifying dignity. It provides financial security without reducing marriage to commercial exchange. It encourages seriousness in entering the marital covenant. Regrettably, social practices have at times undermined these objectives. Nominal dower amounts are occasionally fixed merely to satisfy custom. In other instances, substantial dower is recorded without any genuine intention of performance. Sometimes valuable property is mentioned in the Nikahnama without adequate description or certainty. At other times, husbands acknowledge valuable dower at marriage but subsequently deny the agreement itself. Each of these practices frustrates the philosophy underlying Islamic law. Courts cannot reform social customs by judicial decree. They can, however, ensure that where parties have genuinely agreed upon dower, the right receives effective legal protection, and where ambiguity exists, interpretation is guided by the objectives which Islamic law sought to achieve rather than by technical formalism alone.

It follows that disputes concerning dower must not be approached as ordinary commercial litigation. The Court is not concerned merely with enforcing financial bargains. It is concerned with enforcing one of the principal proprietary rights which Islamic law attaches to marriage. This does not justify abandoning settled principles of evidence. It does require those principles to be applied with due appreciation of the nature of the right in issue. Accordingly, where two interpretations of a matrimonial transaction are reasonably open upon the evidence, the interpretation that best preserves the wife's lawful entitlement, while remaining faithful to the parties' actual agreement and the governing principles of Islamic law, should ordinarily be preferred. Such an approach neither favours one party nor creates new rights. It simply gives meaningful effect to the legal policy unmistakably reflected in the Holy Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the Constitution.

The discussion may be summarised in the following propositions: (i) Dower is a mandatory legal incident of marriage imposed by Islamic law. (ii) It is neither the price of the wife nor consideration in the technical common-law sense. (iii) It constitutes the exclusive proprietary right of the wife. (iv) The institution reflects and reinforces the constitutional values of human dignity, equality before law, protection of the family and fidelity to the injunctions of Islam. (v) Courts must interpret laws affecting dower in a manner that gives practical and effective protection to the wife's lawful entitlement while remaining faithful to the actual agreement proved by the evidence.

We now turn to the legal character of the transaction whereby a husband gives, either before the marriage or at the time of marriage or thereafter, immovable property to his wife in lieu of, wholly or partly, of her dower. The real purpose of this inquiry is not what form the transaction outwardly resembles, but what legal obligation the transaction is intended to discharge. Islamic jurisprudence has consistently attached greater importance to the substance of legal transactions than to the labels assigned to them. Transactions are judged according to their legal reality and intended operation, not merely according to the terminology employed by the parties.16 We are therefore of the view that greater doctrinal clarity is achieved by recognising that the act of giving property derives its legal character from the obligation of dower rather than by forcing it into categories developed for materially different transactions. It is made because Islamic law has already imposed upon the husband an enforceable proprietary liability, which he has elected to satisfy by giving property. In this respect, the transaction bears closer resemblance to performance of an obligation than to the creation of a contractual exchange. The property functions as the agreed medium of dower. We, therefore, consider that the better view is that to give an immovable property in lieu of dower is, in substance and legal effect, a mode of discharging a matrimonial obligation, and its validity, interpretation and enforcement must primarily be governed by the principles regulating dower itself.17 It bears noting that Muslim personal law creates and regulates the obligation of dower. The transfer of ownership in immovable property, however, is also governed by statutory law. Neither body of law operates in isolation. The Court's duty is to harmonise them so that each is given its proper field of operation. It is a settled principle that where one law creates a substantive right and another prescribes the mode by which that right is to be effectuated, the two should ordinarily be read together rather than in conflict. Muslim personal law determines whether a wife has become entitled to property as dower. The general law of property determines how title in that property is legally conveyed and protected.18 16 A famous legal maxim of Islamic Jurisprudence (العبرة في العقود للمقاصد والمعاني ال لأللفاظ والمباني) (In contracts, consideration is given to the objectives and meanings, not merely to the words and forms) 17 Kasani, Badai al-Sania, Vol. 2, P.282 to 297 18 Fazal-ur-Rehman v. Mst. Sosan Jan and others (1989 SCMR 651)

The next question before us concerns the legal character of the Nikahnama itself. Is it the marriage contract from which the parties' rights originate, or is it a statutory record prepared by a public functionary to preserve evidence of a contract already concluded? The answer to that question will determine the proper approach to interpreting ambiguous or inaccurate entries made in the prescribed form of Nikahnama. The answer is of far-reaching importance. If the Nikahnama is itself the contract, every right of the parties must necessarily originate from its contents. If, however, it is merely an official record of a transaction already completed, the Court's function extends beyond reading the document. It must ascertain whether the document faithfully records the agreement actually concluded between the parties.

Under Islamic law, a marriage comes into existence immediately upon a valid offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul) exchanged between legally competent parties in the presence of the witnesses required by law. The legal relationship arises at that very moment. The rights and obligations of the spouses arise at that very moment. The obligation to pay dower likewise arises at that very moment. None of these consequences depends upon the subsequent preparation of a written document. The Nikahnama is ordinarily prepared after the essential ingredients of marriage have already been completed. The parties have agreed. The marriage has been solemnised. The witnesses have attested it. Only thereafter does the Nikah Registrar perform his statutory duty of recording the transaction in the prescribed form, that is, the Nikahnama. Chronology itself demonstrates that the marriage is the juridical source of the rights; the Nikahnama is their official memorial.

Be it noted here that the requirement of maintaining a Nikahnama was introduced not to alter the juristic nature of marriage but to secure certainty, authenticity and public record. The Legislature recognised that matrimonial disputes frequently arose regarding dower, delegated divorce, conditions of marriage and other agreed terms. A contemporaneous written record prepared by an authorised public functionary was therefore intended to minimise subsequent controversy. The statute, the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, sought to improve proof. It did not seek to redefine marriage. The prescribed Nikahnama is therefore an instrument of evidence. It records. It does not create. It certifies. It does not solemnise. It preserves. It does not originate.

The legal position of the Nikah Registrar also deserves careful attention. The Union Council, under section 5 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, grants a licence to any person competent to solemnise a marriage under Muslim Law to act as a Nikah Registrar. He performs public duties.19 He is required to maintain official registers and record the particulars of marriages in the manner prescribed by law.20 He is not, however, a party to the marriage contract and has no authority to negotiate its terms on behalf of either spouse. His function is ministerial, though undoubtedly important. The Nikah Registrar neither determines the amount of dower nor decides the conditions upon which the parties agree. The spouses or their authorised representatives settle those matters before or at the time of the solemnisation of marriage. The Nikah Registrar's duty is to faithfully reduce those agreed terms into the prescribed Nikahnama. His authority is evidentiary, not creative.

To emphasise what we have stated above, it may also be noted that every legal system recognises a distinction between a legal transaction and the document recording it. A contract for sale exists because the parties agree. A deed records or effectuates that agreement according to law. A judgment records the decision of the Court. The judgment is not the dispute. Likewise, a birth certificate records a birth; it does not bring the child into existence. The Nikahnama belongs to the same evidentiary category. It is evidence of the marriage. It is not the marriage contract itself.

We have thus identified the legal character of the Nikahnama. The remaining question concerns the evidentiary principles governing its use and the methodology by which ambiguous entries in the Nikahnama are to be interpreted. Since that issue affects not only disputes relating to dower but every material stipulation contained in the Nikahnama, it calls for the formulation of clear principles capable of uniform application by the Courts throughout the country. 19 Muhammad Arif v. Muhammad Kawshar Ali (PLD 1969 SC 435) 20 Sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 read with Rule 8 of the Rules under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961

A Nikahnama is both a private and a public document in different senses. It records a private transaction between two individuals.21 It is, however, prepared in the manner prescribed by statute. A public officer completes it. It forms part of an official register maintained under law. The law therefore attaches public importance to its preparation and preservation. Even so, its public character does not alter the source of the rights recorded therein. The rights continue to arise from the agreement of the parties as recognised by Islamic law. The statutory record merely preserves evidence of those rights. Accordingly, the interpretation of the Nikahnama must simultaneously respect two objectives: first, preserving the integrity of official records; and secondly, giving effect to the actual consensus of the parties. Neither objective should be sacrificed unnecessarily in favour of the other.22

Being prepared by a public functionary in the discharge of statutory duties, the Nikahnama enjoys a presumption of regularity.23 Courts ordinarily presume that official acts have been regularly performed.24 Consequently, the entries made by the Nikah Registrar constitute prima facie evidence of the matters recorded therein. The presumption is an important one. It promotes certainty. It protects public confidence in official records. It discourages frivolous challenges. Nevertheless, the presumption is not conclusive. It is rebuttable. The law has never regarded official records as infallible. Public officers may misunderstand instructions. They may omit particulars. They may employ inaccurate language. They may commit clerical errors. The purpose of the presumption is to facilitate proof, not to perpetuate injustice.

Experience demonstrates that many matrimonial disputes arise not because the parties failed to reach agreement but because the agreement was imperfectly recorded. Several factors contribute to this difficulty. The Nikahnama is completed under circumstances that are often informal. The parties are ordinarily not trained in law. The Nikah Registrar frequently records legal concepts causally. Many entries are made in haste. Some columns are left 21 Fazal ur Rehman v. Mst. Sosan Jan and others (1989 SCMR 651) 22 Performance Industries Ltd. v. Sylvan Lake Golf & Tennis Club Ltd., [2002] 1 S.C.R. 678 23 Ashiq Ali and others v. Mst. Zamir Fatima and others (PLD 2004 SC 10) 24 Art. 129, Qanun-e-Shahadat, 1984. blank. Others are completed without fully appreciating their legal significance. Occasionally, ambiguous expressions are employed to describe valuable immovable property. None of these possibilities may be ignored by the Court. Under the scheme of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, and the rules made thereunder, the Nikah Registrar is not expected to adjudicate disputes. His function is administrative. He records what he is told. The possibility of recording error is therefore inherent in the statutory scheme.

It would be contrary to both justice and common sense to hold that every inaccuracy committed by the Nikah Registrar automatically destroys rights genuinely agreed upon by the parties. Such an approach would subordinate substance to form. It would make the statutory record superior to the transaction which it was designed merely to preserve. The law does not favour such inversion. Equally unacceptable would be the opposite approach, whereby every dissatisfied litigant is permitted to disregard the Nikahnama upon making a bare allegation that it does not reflect the true agreement. Such an approach would undermine the very certainty which the statutory record was intended to achieve. The law must therefore strike an appropriate balance.25 We accordingly hold that the Nikahnama occupies a dual evidentiary position. It is the primary documentary evidence26 of the terms of the marriage. Ordinarily, the Court shall begin with the language employed in the Nikahnama. Where that language is clear, complete and free from ambiguity, it ordinarily furnishes the best evidence of the parties' agreement. Where, however, the language is reasonably capable of more than one interpretation, is internally inconsistent, contains obvious omissions, inaccurately describes the subject matter, or is challenged by cogent evidence demonstrating that it does not faithfully record the actual agreement, the Court is not confined to the document alone. It may receive admissible evidence directed to ascertaining the true consensus of the parties.27 25 Frederick E. Rose (London) Ltd. v. William H. Pim Jnr. & Co. Ltd (1953) QB 450 and Crane v. The burden of displacing the presumption attached to the Nikahnama rests upon the party asserting that the document does not correctly record the transaction. A mere denial is insufficient. A party faced with such a situation would be obliged to plead the true agreement with all its essential details; identify the erroneous or ambiguous entries; produce evidence of the parties’ common intention; explain that the mistake originated with the Nikah Registrar; and seek an interpretation consistent with the parties’ actual agreement.28 The evidence to be presented must be clear, convincing and consistent. The greater the departure sought from the official record, the heavier becomes the evidentiary burden. Whenever such a dispute arises, the Court should ordinarily proceed in the following sequence: First, determine whether the disputed entry is clear or genuinely ambiguous. Secondly, ascertain the source of the ambiguity, including whether it arose from the Nikahnama, the Nikah Registrar, the parties themselves, or subsequent events. Thirdly, where ambiguity genuinely exists, consider admissible evidence relating to the circumstances prevailing at the time of marriage. Fourthly, evaluate subsequent conduct only insofar as it reliably reflects the parties' original intention. Fifthly, prefer the interpretation that best harmonises all parts of the Nikahnama rather than rendering any material entry meaningless. Sixthly, adopt the interpretation which most faithfully gives effect to the actual agreement of the parties, provided it is consistent with Islamic law and the applicable statutory provisions. This approach neither weakens the evidentiary value of the Nikahnama nor diminishes the authority of the Nikah Registrar. On the contrary, it preserves the integrity of the statutory scheme by recognising that official records exist to serve justice rather than to defeat it. The law protects documents because they ordinarily record the truth. It does not require courts to ignore the truth merely because the document is imperfect. 28 Crane v. Hegeman-Harris Co. It is important to reiterate that family disputes differ fundamentally from commercial litigation. The purpose of adjudication is not merely to identify technical defects in documentation. It is to administer justice within relationships that frequently involve unequal bargaining power, limited legal advice and documents prepared by public officials in informal settings. Excessive technicality is therefore particularly inappropriate where it defeats rights clearly intended to be created. This does not mean that courts are at liberty to rewrite the Nikahnama according to subjective notions of fairness. Judicial interpretation is not judicial legislation. The Court cannot create obligations never undertaken. Nor can it deprive one party of rights clearly reserved by lawful agreement. The object remains faithful interpretation, not benevolent reconstruction. We accordingly hold that where a material entry in the Nikahnama is reasonably capable of more than one meaning, or where the Nikahnama fails adequately to record the transaction actually concluded by the parties, the Court shall interpret the document by reading its language in light of the surrounding circumstances, the conduct of the parties, the objectives of the law relating to marriage and dower, and the constitutional principles protecting dignity, justice and the family, always striving to give effect to the true agreement proved by the evidence rather than to an accidental imperfection in the statutory record.

It is now necessary to examine the relationship between Columns 13, 14, 15 and 16 of the Nikahnama. These columns are presented in the following manner in the Nikahnama prescribed in the rules under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961: A review of these columns shows that all relate to dower, though each addresses a distinct aspect of it. They are complementary rather than contradictory. Before examining these provisions in more detail, however, two elementary principles concerning dower must be kept “13. Amount of dower :_______________ 14. How much of the dower is mu’ajjal (prompt) and how much mu’wajjal (deferred) :_______________ 15. Whether any portion of the dower was paid at the time of marriage, if so, how much :_______________ 16. Whether any property was given in lieu of the whole or any portion of the dower with specification of the same and its valuation agreed to between the parties :_______________” in view. First, in Islamic law there is no maximum limit prescribed for dower. Accordingly, any lawful object having value may be settled as dower. It may, therefore, take the form of cash, merchandise, goods, gold, jewellery, movable or immovable property, shares in a company, dividends, or any other lawful asset of value. Second, the amount or subject matter of dower may be fixed at any time before the marriage, at the time of marriage, or even after the marriage, so long as the marriage subsists. It may also be increased during the subsistence of the marriage.29 With these principles in mind, we turn to the relevant columns of the Nikahnama, which is prescribed in the English language and is contained in Form II of the Rules framed under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. Column 13 records the amount of dower. It is important to clarify at the outset its three important aspects: first, the words “amount of dower” are not preceded by the word “total”, which means the amount of dower stated in this column does not represent the whole existing dower. The second is that the word “amount” is used here as a noun, which, according to the Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary of Current English, means the quantity of something. Therefore, the words “amount of dower” refer to the quantity of dower. The third is that translating the word "amount" into Urdu as " رقم" (“raqam”) may, in certain contexts, be misleading. The word " رقم" (“raqam”) is commonly understood to denote cash, and if construed narrowly, it may unduly restrict the concept of dower to monetary consideration alone, whereas under Islamic law and the statutory scheme, dower may consist of any lawful object of value. Such a restrictive interpretation would not be consistent with the underlying legal principles governing dower. In substance, Column 13 requires the Nikah Registrar to record the dower correctly agreed between the parties, which may consist of cash, movable or immovable property, gold, jewellery, or any other lawful object of value. Column 14 specifies what portion of the dower is prompt (mu'ajjal) and what portion is deferred (mu'wajjal). Column 15 records whether any portion of the dower was paid at the time of marriage and, if so, the amount or value thereof. Column 16 records whether any property is given in lieu of the whole or any portion of the dower, together with a 29 Mian Aziz A. Sheikh v. The Commissioner of Income Tax Investigation, Lahore (PLD 1989 SC 613), Mst. Naziran Begum through LRs v. Mst. Khurshid Begum through LRs (1999 SCMR 1171), and Ghania Hassan v. Shahid Hussain Shahid and another (2016 SCMR 2170) specification of that property and the valuation agreed upon by the parties. At this juncture, four features of Column 16 are particularly significant. First, the words "at the time of marriage", which expressly appear in Column 15, are not in Column 16. This omission is not without purpose; it may signify a transaction that had not taken place at the time of marriage. It is equally possible that it is related to that dower that was agreed upon at the time of marriage. That is why it has been couched in a language that is unfettered by the constraints of time. Second, Column 16 refers to "property", which may be of any kind, whether movable or immovable. Third, it requires the property given in lieu of the whole or any portion of the dower to be specifically identified, together with its valuation as agreed between the parties. Fourth, it does not stipulate that the dower mentioned in it is an alternative arrangement to the dower listed in Columns 13, 14 and 15. Neither excludes the other. If the legislature intended this, it would have stated it explicitly. The omission regarding this point is deliberate and meaningful. Thus, a harmonious reading of these columns suggests that the dower specified within them collectively represents the total amount of dower agreed upon. As such, the view expressed in Naheed Begum and Fakhara Jabeen with regard to these columns is hereby clarified and further explained, albeit in a somewhat different tone and with certain modifications.

There is, however, an additional issue that frequently arises in proceedings for the recovery of dower. Our attention has been drawn, based on empirical study and experience, to instances where a husband gives, and records in the Nikahnama or Kabinnama as dower, immovable property which he neither owns nor possesses, or he partially owns and possesses the property, or where he gives property without providing its details and descriptions. There are also instances where the property so given is the subject matter of litigation, and the husband subsequently loses his title thereto as a consequence of such proceedings. It is to be noted here that when the parties agree that an immovable property shall be given to the wife in lieu of, or towards satisfaction of, dower, such an entry in the Nikahnama ordinarily evidences an agreement or undertaking to transfer the property. Therefore, in the circumstances described above, the husband cannot be permitted to defeat his undertaking and the wife's entitlement to dower merely because the property specified in the Nikahnama could not ultimately be transferred to or retained by her. The inability to transfer the property cannot, by itself, extinguish the underlying obligation to pay the dower. The husband must remain liable to discharge that obligation. It would, therefore, be appropriate to hold that where immovable property has been stipulated as dower but ultimately cannot be transferred to the wife, the husband remains liable to satisfy the dower obligation by paying the value of the immovable property expressly agreed between the parties and recorded in the Nikahnama. Where no such value has been agreed or recorded, the Court may determine the value of the property on the basis of its market value prevailing at the time of decree or adjudication of the wife's claim for recovery of dower. Such an approach preserves the substance of the parties’ agreement, prevents the husband from taking advantage of his own inability or failure to transfer the property, and, most importantly, ensures the effective enforcement of the wife’s vested entitlement to dower.30

The foregoing principles answer the interpretive issues. It now remains to synthesise the conclusions reached throughout this judgment into clear answers to the questions formulated and to issue such directions as may be necessary for the guidance of Courts, Nikah Registrars and other authorities entrusted with the administration of Muslim family law. This is important because it concerns not merely the interpretation of a particular Nikahnama, but the proper legal methodology for construing a statutory marriage document. The entries in different columns cannot be read in isolation; they must be harmonised so that every entry is given effect, if reasonably possible. No single column should ordinarily be treated as overriding another. A Nikahnama is prepared by a public functionary on a prescribed statutory form. Any ambiguity or inconsistency in the entries is, therefore, not to be visited upon the spouses without first attempting a harmonious construction consistent with Islamic law, the intention of the parties, and the surrounding circumstances. 30 Rustam Ali v. Mehreen Mansoor and others (PLD 2020 SC 269)

Before parting, we wish to emphasise that we must not allow the institution of marriage to be reduced to a transaction where the wife's rights are an afterthought. We must not allow husband to treat dower as a weapon to be used in later disputes. I will pay you if you behave; I will pay you if you do not ask for divorce. That is not dower. That is coercion. True dower is given with a good heart, at the time agreed, without conditions that demean the wife. And when it is not given, the courts must step in, not with hesitation, not with apology, but with the full authority of the law. Because to fail to enforce dower is to tell every woman in this jurisdiction that her rights are theoretical. It is to tell every man that he can make promises before Allah and before the law and then ignore them. It is to weaken the family and, through the family, to weaken the nation. Therefore, in every case that comes before a court involving dower, the court must begin with this premise: the wife's dignity is at stake. Her right is not a favour. It is a command of the Shari'ah, a command of the statute, and a command of justice. The Court's task is to determine, on evidence, what that right is, and then to ensure that it is fulfilled. Let no husband think that he can escape this liability by silence. Let no court think that it can dispose of this matter lightly. For in protecting dower, we are protecting the home. By protecting the home, we protect society. And in protecting society, we are fulfilling the promise of a nation that claims to be founded on the principles of Islam, justice, and human dignity. The law is clear. The religion is clear. The conscience of society is clear. What remains is only the determination of fact: what was the dower, and how did the husband agree to pay it? Once that is determined, the decree must follow, and it must be enforced with grace if the husband complies, and with the full force of law if he does not. That is the only way to ensure that the dignity of a wife, which begins at the Nikah, is protected until the very end.
