They further lay down the procedure for revision proceedings, regulate the preservation and inspection of records, the issuance of certified copies, the payment of prescribed fees, and the institution of complaints for offences under the Ordinance and the Rules. 17. The controversy in the present case centres on the interpretation of the columns of the prescribed Nikahnama. The starting point for determining its legal significance is Section 5 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, which makes the registration of every Muslim 49 The Muslim Family Laws Rules, 1961 marriage compulsory and authorizes the prescription of the form of the Nikahnama, the registers to be maintained by Nikah Registrars, the records to be preserved by the Union Council, and the procedure for registration. Rule 8 gives effect to this statutory scheme by requiring every licensed Nikah Registrar to record marriages only in the official bound register of Nikahnamas supplied by the Union Council. The prescribed Nikahnama is, therefore, not a document prepared at the discretion of the parties but a statutory form prescribed under the authority of the Ordinance. 18. It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that a form appended to a statute or contained in a Schedule is ordinarily intended to serve as a model or guide and cannot be permitted to override, enlarge or restrict the clear language of the substantive/enacting provision. Where there is any inconsistency between the enacting part of the statute and the prescribed form, the former must prevail. Such forms may, however, be consulted as an aid to construction where they throw light upon the meaning or operation of the substantive provision. The position would be different where the statute itself makes compliance with the prescribed form imperative, or the language of the form clearly indicates that strict adherence was intended; in such circumstances, the form assumes a mandatory character and must be followed accordingly.50 19. Within the framework of the Ordinance, the prescribed Nikahnama occupies a distinct legal position. Its use is mandatory, and compliance with the prescribed form is a statutory obligation imposed upon every Nikah Registrar. More importantly, the Nikahnama constitutes the official record of the marriage contract. Prepared at the time of the marriage and signed by the spouses, the witnesses, and the Nikah Registrar, it records the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon by the parties. Being prepared in the prescribed statutory form and preserved as an official public record, it carries substantial evidentiary value unless its contents are successfully challenged in accordance with law. It follows that every column of the prescribed Nikahnama must be given its due and meaningful effect. The legislature cannot be presumed to have incorporated separate columns without purpose. Each column is intended to record a distinct aspect of the marriage contract and must be interpreted according to its language, the intention of the parties, and the principles of Muslim law coupled 50 Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, Bengal v. Keshab Chandra Mandal AIR 1950 Supreme Court 265, Swaranath Bhatia AIR 1948 Mad 427, Banarsi Das Vs. The Cane Commissioner and Ors. AIR 1963 Supreme Court 1417 with pleadings of the parties. No entry can be treated as redundant or insignificant unless the statute expressly provides otherwise. 20. The prescribed Nikahnama is, therefore, much more than a document for the registration of marriage. It is a statutory instrument forming an integral part of the legal framework established by the Ordinance, 1961 and the Rules framed thereunder. At the same time, it is the authentic record of the marriage contract, preserving the rights and obligations agreed upon by the spouses and serving as the primary documentary evidence for resolving disputes concerning the terms of their marriage. 21. So far as the columns of the Nikahnama are concerned, they form the substantial question of law before this Court. A careful reading of the prescribed Nikahnama shows that its columns are arranged in a systematic sequence. Columns 1 to 6 relate to the place where the Nikah is solemnized and record the particulars of the spouses, including their names, parentage, age, and marital status, i.e., whether they are unmarried or previously married. Columns 7 to 11 deal with the essential requirements of a valid Nikah by providing for the names of the witnesses and, where applicable, the name of the Wakeel appointed on behalf of either spouse. Column 12 simply records the date on which the Nikah was solemnized. The real controversy in the present case centres on Columns 13 to 16, which deal with the fixation of dower (Mahr). The prescribed form does not treat dower as a single entry; instead, it divides the subject into four separate columns, each intended to record a different aspect of the parties' agreement. In practice, however, these columns are often filled in mechanically, without appreciating the distinct purpose each of them serves, even though the language used in the form is plain and self-explanatory. 22. Lastly, Column 17 may be used to record conditions relating to the mutual rights and responsibilities of the spouses and other aspects of their married life. Such conditions may regulate or qualify the exercise of a right belonging to either party, but they cannot altogether extinguish or deprive a party of a lawful right. The conditions may be limited to a specified period or may continue throughout the subsistence of the marriage. They should be expressed in clear and unambiguous terms so as to avoid uncertainty or difficulties in their interpretation and enforcement. 23. Moving further, Column 18 deals with the question whether the husband has delegated to the wife the right to pronounce Talaq and, if so, the conditions subject to which that right may be exercised. This relates to Talaq-e-Tafweez (delegated divorce), under which the husband confers upon the wife the authority to pronounce Talaq on his behalf. Such delegation is ordinarily recorded in Column 18 of the Nikahnama. Unlike the husband's inherent right to pronounce Talaq, the wife's authority under Talaq-e-Tafweez exists only where it has been expressly delegated and incorporated into the marriage contract. The object of this arrangement is to enable the wife, in appropriate circumstances, to dissolve the marriage where its continuation has become untenable, without being entirely dependent upon the husband's willingness to pronounce Talaq. Likewise, Column 19 asks whether any restriction has been placed on the husband's right to pronounce Talaq. The legal position in this regard is well settled. This Court, in case of Tania Bibi51 in line with the settled principles of Islamic jurisprudence, held that the husband retains the right to pronounce Talaq, and that any condition which seeks to take away, prohibit, or completely restrict the exercise of that right is void and without legal effect. 24. Similarly, Column 20 asks whether any separate written instrument relating to dower, maintenance, or any other matrimonial matter was executed at the time of the marriage. Columns 21, 22, and 23 relate to the husband's marital status. They require disclosure of whether he has any existing wife, the number of children from such marriage, and whether prior permission to contract another marriage, where required, was obtained from the concerned Union Council. Finally, Columns 24 to 26 deal with the particulars of the Nikah Registrar (Nikah Khawan), the date of registration of the marriage, and the registration fee paid in accordance with the provisions of the parent statute. 25. At the conclusion of the Nikahnama, the spouses, the witnesses to the marriage, and the other persons required under the prescribed form append their signatures along with the necessary particulars, thereby completing the execution of the Nikahnama. Once registered, the Nikahnama serves as proof of the marriage and is admissible as evidence in legal proceedings concerning the marriage. It records the facts and conditions of the Nikah as agreed upon by the parties and reflected in its prescribed columns. 26. As the controversy before this Court pertains to entries Nos. 13 to 16 of the Nikahnama, which relate to dower, it is appropriate, at the outset, to examine the concept and nature of dower in the light of the injunctions of the Holy Quran, the Sunnah and Ahadith of the Holy 51 Tania Bibi v. Muhammad Arif 2008 SCMR 186 Prophet (PBUH), the applicable law, and the judicial precedents laid down by this Court from time to time. 27. One of the important features of a Muslim marriage is Mahr, commonly known as Dower or Haq Mehr. It is a right that a wife acquires from the very inception of the marriage and is payable by the husband. The Arabic term Al-Mahr refers to this right, which Allah (S.W.T.) has granted to women and made binding upon the husband. It is, therefore, not simply a customary payment or a voluntary gift; rather, it is a recognized obligation arising from the marital relationship and belongs exclusively to the wife. In its essence, Mahr is a gift that the husband is obliged to give to his wife at the time of marriage. It carries a deeper meaning, as it reflects the husband's sincerity, affection, and commitment towards the marital relationship. The Holy Quran recognizes the wife's entitlement to dower and directs that it be given to her willingly and graciously. Once it becomes due, the wife alone has the right to receive and deal with it, and neither the husband nor his family can claim ownership over it. The amount of Mahr and the manner in which it is to be paid may be agreed upon by the parties. Depending upon the terms of the marriage, it may be payable immediately or may be deferred until a later time or event. This distinction only relates to the timing of payment and does not diminish the wife's underlying right to receive it. More importantly, Mahr recognizes the wife as an independent holder of property and financial rights. It provides her with something that belongs to her in her own right and over which she may exercise ownership according to law. In this sense, Mahr is not merely a financial transaction accompanying marriage; it is an expression of the respect, dignity, and security that Islamic law seeks to secure for a woman within the marital relationship. Muslim jurists and scholars have explained and defined the concept of Mahr or Dower in different ways. Some of the notable definitions are set out below: ‘Dower is a consideration which belongs absolutely to Wife.’52 ‘Dower is the sum of money or other property which a wife is entitled to receive from Husband in consideration of marriage.’53 ‘Dower is that financial gain which the wife is entitled to receive from her husband by virtue of the marriage contract itself whether named or not in the contract of marriage.’54 ‘Dower, under the Mahammadan Law, is a sum of money or other property promised by the husband to be paid or delivered to the 52 Ameer Ali 53 DF. Mulla 54 Dr. Tanzil Ur Rahman, 1978, p. 218 wife in consideration of the marriage, and even where no dower is excessively fixed or mentioned at the marriage ceremony, the law confers the right of dower upon the wife.’55 ‘Dower is not a consideration proceeding from the Husband for the contract of marriage. But it is an obligation imposed by law on Husband as a mark of respect for the wife, as it is evident from the fact that non-specification of Dower does not affect the validity of marriage.’56 The dower’s importance under Islamic law is evidenced from the fact that it satisfies various functions which leads to the success and prosperity of the marital relationship in between the spouses. The Holy Quran expressly recognizes the obligation of dower and provides guidance in the following words: ‘and give the women (on marriage) their dower as a free gift, but if they, of their own good pleasure, remit any part of it for you, take it and enjoy it with cheer.’57 ‘wed them with their leave, and give them their dowers according to what is reasonable.’58 The above verses of the Holy Quran clearly establish the right of a woman to receive Mahr and, at the same time, mark a clear departure from the practices relating to dower that existed in the pre-Islamic era. The use of the word “give” in the imperative form is particularly significant, as it conveys a direct and obligatory command upon the husband to pay the dower to his wife. It is also noteworthy that, although marriage is a relationship of mutual interest and companionship between the spouses, Islamic law places the financial obligation of Mahr upon the husband. Thus, while the husband is required to give Mahr to the wife from his own means as an incident of marriage, the wife is under no corresponding obligation to pay anything to the husband for entering into the marital relationship. This arrangement reflects the recognition accorded by Islamic law to the wife's independent financial right and dignity within the institution of marriage. The Sunnah of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) further affirms a woman’s right to dower. Ibn Abbas (RA) narrates that: ‘When Hazrat Ali (RA) got married to Hazrat Fatima (RA), the Holy Prophet (PBUH) said to him. Give her something as a (dower). Hazrat Ali (RA) replied: I have nothing with me. The Prophet 55 Abdul Kadir v. Salima, (1886) ILR 8 ALL 149 56 The Principles of Muhammadan Jurisprudence by, Abdul Rahim 57 The Holy Quran, 4:4. 58 The Holy Quran, 4:25. asked: Where is your Hutaimiyyah Shield? I said: It is with me. He said: Give it to her.’59 This indicates that Hazrat Ali (RA) was required to give her something, even if of little material value, such as a shield or any other symbolic gift, with the intention of acknowledging her right and bringing her happiness. There is another Hadith narrated by Hazrat Abu Salama (RA) that: ‘I asked Hazrat Aisha (RA): How much (amount) had Allah’s Messenger (PBUH) given as dower to his wives? She replied: His (dower) to his wives was twelve ‘uqiyyas and one nash. She asked, Do you know what a nash was? I replied: No. She said: it was half an ‘uqiyyas; so the total was five hundred dirhams and that was the Holy Prophet’s dower to his wives.’60 In Islamic jurisprudence, dower (mahr) is a mandatory financial right that every wife acquires by virtue of a valid marriage. It is a gift that the husband is under a legal and religious obligation to give to his wife as a mark of honour, respect and recognition of her status in marriage. The right belongs exclusively to the wife, and neither her father nor any other family member has a claim over it. Because dower is her independent legal right, she may insist upon its payment. 28. The Islamic law does not prescribe any maximum limit for the amount of Mahr that may be given to a woman. Neither the Holy Quran nor the Sunnah of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) lays down a fixed upper limit for dower. The amount may, therefore, be determined according to the husband's financial capacity and the circumstances of the parties. A husband may agree to a higher or lower amount, depending upon his means, family circumstances, customs, traditions, and prevailing practices. What is important, however, is that the dower should have some recognized value. It may consist of money, property (moveable or immoveable), or any other thing having lawful value. The essential requirement is that the subject matter of Mahr must be lawful under Islamic law. If the parties agree upon something prohibited by Allah (S.W.T.), as dower, such an agreement would not constitute a valid Mahr, although the marriage itself would remain valid. In such circumstances, the wife would be entitled to a proper dower equivalent to that ordinarily received by women of similar status in her family or circumstances, in accordance with the principles of Shari‘ah. 29. As discussed above, Muslim jurists are agreed that there is no maximum limit to the amount of Mahr. They, however, differ on the 59 SunanAl-Nasa’i, Book: 26, Kitab Al-Nikah, Hadith: 180. 60 Sunan Ibn Majah, Book:9, KitabAl Nikah, Hadith: 1960. question of its minimum amount, with three principal views emerging among the schools of Islamic jurisprudence. According to the Hanafi jurists, the minimum amount of Mahr is ten dirhams, and a wife should not receive less than this amount. The Maliki jurists, on the other hand, prescribe a minimum of one-quarter of a dinar in gold or three dirhams of pure silver. The Shafi‘i and Hanbali jurists, however, take a different view. They do not prescribe any fixed minimum amount for Mahr. According to them, anything having monetary or recognized value, or anything that can lawfully be used to purchase goods, may constitute valid Mahr. Thus, while the three schools differ as to the minimum amount, they agree on the fundamental principle that Mahr is an essential right of the wife arising from the marriage contract. 30. A practice has increasingly developed in our society whereby an unusually high amount of Mahr is mentioned in the marriage documents, primarily to enhance the prestige or glorify the status of the family. In such cases, however, the parties may privately agree that the publicly stated amount is not intended to be enforced, and that the actual dower payable would be the amount privately settled between them. This practice is referred to as the principle of As-Sum‘at.61 Consequently, where the wife subsequently seeks recovery of the publicly stated amount of Mahr, she may rely upon the documentary record reflecting that amount. The husband, on the other hand, may dispute that the publicly stated amount was ever intended to be payable and may seek to establish the privately agreed amount by producing appropriate evidence in support of his plea. 31. Islamic jurisprudence primarily classifies Mahr on the basis of its fixation into two categories: specified dower (Mahr-i-Musamma) and proper or customary dower (Mahr-i-Misl). Specified dower is the amount mutually agreed upon by the parties at the time of Nikah or subsequently by their consent. The parties may agree to increase the amount, and the quantum may vary according to their circumstances, financial position, family background and prevailing customs. Proper or customary dower, on the other hand, becomes relevant where no amount has been specified at the time of marriage or where the stipulated dower cannot legally take effect. In such circumstances, the wife's entitlement is determined with reference to the dower ordinarily received by women of similar standing, particularly those belonging to her paternal family, such as her sisters, paternal aunts and other comparable female relatives. The wife's personal circumstances and 61 Nasir Ahmad Khan v. Mst. Ismat Jehan Begum PLD 1969 Supreme Court 194 qualities, including her age, education, intelligence, beauty and social position, may also be taken into account, along with the financial condition of the husband and the customs and prevailing conditions of the society. The underlying principle is that the wife should receive “dower among her equals”; thus, even where the parties have failed to specify an amount, the law provides a basis for determining a fair and appropriate Mahr having regard to the circumstances of the wife and the parties. 32. With respect to the time of payment, specified dower is generally divided into prompt dower (mu’ajjal) and deferred dower (mu’wajjal, or ghair mu’ajjal). Prompt dower becomes payable immediately upon marriage and may be demanded by the wife at any time thereafter, whether before or after consummation. Its essential characteristic is that, once demanded, it is payable without further delay. Until the prompt dower is paid, the wife may, in appropriate circumstances, refuse to enter into or continue the marital relationship. Deferred dower, on the other hand, is an amount whose payment is postponed until a future date, an agreed event or a circumstance recognized by law. The parties may specify the time or condition of payment in the Nikahnama. Traditionally, where no particular time was fixed, deferred dower becomes payable upon the dissolution of marriage by divorce or upon the death of either spouse. The distinguishing feature of deferred dower is its time of payment. Until the agreed time or event for its payment occurs, the wife ordinarily cannot demand it as a presently due amount. The husband, however, may, if he chooses, pay the deferred dower earlier and thereby discharge his obligation before its normal maturity.62 Thus, the postponement affects the time when the wife can enforce payment, but does not take away her substantive right to the dower. The wife’s right in deferred dower is, therefore, a vested right rather than a contingent one. If she dies before the deferred amount becomes payable, the right does not disappear with her; it forms part of her estate and may be claimed by her heirs. Similarly, where the parties have expressly agreed that the deferred dower may be paid earlier, such an agreement would ordinarily govern the time of payment. In this way, deferred dower serves a dual purpose: it secures the wife’s financial right while also placing upon the husband a continuing obligation arising from the Nikahnama, payment of which ordinarily becomes enforceable upon the agreed maturity of the dower. The distinction between prompt and deferred dower concerns the time of payment, rather than the 62 Syed Sajjad Hussain v. Judge Family Court and Others 2019 CLC 1462, Muhammad Qayyum Anjum v. ADJ etc 2022 MLD 416 existence of the wife's right. Her right to Mahr arises from the marriage itself, while the agreed terms determine when that right becomes enforceable for payment. Deferred dower may therefore be payable upon a specified condition, divorce or death.63 Where the parties do not specify the nature of the dower, i.e., whether it is prompt or deferred, then, the entire dower is treated as prompt.64 Thus, the absence of an express stipulation does not deprive the wife of her right to dower; rather, the law determines the time of payment according to the applicable principles. Likewise, an exception to the general rule governing deferred dower arises where a man contracts another marriage during the subsistence of an existing marriage without obtaining the prior written permission of the Arbitration Council. In such circumstances, the entire amount of dower, whether prompt or deferred, becomes immediately due and payable to his existing wife or wives.65 Importantly, dower becomes due and remains unpaid, it constitutes a financial obligation or debt owed by the husband to the wife. Thus, while Islamic law allows the parties considerable flexibility in determining when dower is to be paid, the wife's proprietary right remains protected throughout. Whether the amount is payable immediately, on demand, after an agreed period, or upon dissolution of marriage, Mahr remains an enforceable obligation belonging exclusively to the wife. 33. So far as the controversy relating to entries of dower is concerned, it may be noted that the Nikahnama contains four columns, i.e., Columns 13 to 16, relating to the fixation and payment of dower. However, all four columns are not necessarily applicable in every case; their applicability depends upon the terms agreed upon by the parties and the circumstances of each marriage. It is, therefore, appropriate to examine the scope and purpose of each column separately. Column 13 of the Nikahnama begins with the words ‘Amount of dower.’ The use of the word ‘amount’ should not, however, be understood in a narrow sense as referring only to cash or a specific monetary sum. The expression is of general import and may encompass the value of property or other assets agreed to be given as dower, whether movable or immovable. The ordinary meaning of the word ‘Amount’ also supports such a broader understanding, as defined in the dictionary in the following terms: ‘the total of something in number, size, value, or 63 Saadia Usman and another v. Muhammad Usman Iqbal Jadoon and another 2009 SCMR 64 S. 10 of Muslim Family Law Ordinance, 1961 and Khalid Pervaiz v. Samina and others 2024 SCMR 142 65 S. 6(5)(a) of the Ordinance, 1961. extent’66. Accordingly, this column should comprehensively reflect the entire dower agreed to be given by the husband to the wife, whether payable as prompt or deferred dower, and whether consisting of movable or immovable property. Column 14, headed “How much of the dower is mu’wajjal (prompt) and how much ghair mu’wajjal (deferred)”, requires the parties to specify how the total dower mentioned in Column 13 is to be divided between prompt (mu’ajjal) and deferred (ghair mu’ajjal/mu’wajjal) dower. It should, therefore, clearly indicate the portion payable immediately and the portion whose payment is deferred. Where the parties have not agreed upon any such division, the position should be expressly recorded in the Nikahnama. In the absence of a stipulation distinguishing between prompt and deferred dower, the entire dower is treated as prompt and becomes payable on demand. Column 15, headed “Whether any portion of the dower was paid at the time of marriage, if so, how much,” relates to the payment of the dower mentioned in Column 13 at the time of Nikah. Where any part of the dower, or the entire amount, has actually been paid at the time of solemnization of the marriage, the fact and the amount so paid should be clearly recorded in this column. Since the entry concerns an actual payment, due care should be taken to ensure that the amount recorded has in fact been paid before the relevant entry is made in the Nikahnama. Column 16, headed “Whether any property was given in lieu of the whole or any portion of the dower with specification of the same and its valuation agreed to between the parties,” is intended to record any movable or immovable property agreed to be given as Mahr, whether in substitution for, or in satisfaction of, the whole or any part of the dower specified in Column 13. Where property is agreed to be given as dower, its particulars should be stated with sufficient clarity, including its description, measurements, nature, location and the value mutually agreed upon by the parties. Accurate recording of these particulars is important, as it facilitates the identification and enforcement of the wife's entitlement to the property. 34. Importantly, the Nikahnama is a statutory form, and due regard must therefore be given to all of its entries. Its meaning and effect should be gathered from the document as a whole, particularly by reading together the entry relating to the total dower with those dealing with its nature, mode and timing of payment. The statutory scheme shows that these entries are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Each serves a specific purpose, but, when read together, they present the 66 Concise Oxford English Dictionary, 11th ed., ed. Catherine Soanes and Angus Stevenson (Oxford University Press, 2008) complete picture of the parties’ agreement concerning Mahr. Accordingly, the entries should be given their ordinary meaning and interpreted harmoniously so that effect is given to the transaction recorded in the Nikahnama, rather than allowing one entry to override, nullify or render another redundant. In this regard, the proper approach is to treat Columns 13 to 16 as interrelated components of a single statutory scheme governing dower. The entry concerning property cannot, therefore, be regarded as wholly independent of the other dower-related entries, nor can it invariably be treated as subordinate to them. Its legal effect must be determined in the context of the dower agreed between the parties and the Nikahnama read as a whole. The intention of the parties is undoubtedly material, but such intention must be objectively ascertained from the Nikahnama as a whole, read in conjunction with the pleadings of the parties and the evidence led in support thereof, rather than being inferred merely from an isolated entry or a subsequent unilateral assertion of either spouse. Such an approach respects the statutory character of the Nikahnama while, at the same time, giving due effect to the actual agreement of the parties and protecting the wife’s proprietary entitlement to Mahr. 35. It is not out of place to observe that the law provides a complete statutory mechanism for filling in the columns of the Nikahnama and expressly casts the corresponding duty upon the Nikah Registrar. The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 places the registration of every marriage solemnized under Muslim law within a statutory framework. Section 5 provides for the appointment of licensed Nikah Registrars by the Union Council, ordinarily one for each Ward. Under the Rules, any person competent to solemnize a marriage may apply for a licence, which may be granted by the Union Council after satisfying itself that the applicant is a fit and proper person. The licence remains permanent unless revoked for violation of its conditions. The Nikah Registrar is not merely a person who records a marriage; he is a statutory functionary entrusted with maintaining an authentic official record of the marriage. He is supplied with the prescribed Nikahnama register and official seal and, where he solemnizes the marriage, is required to complete the prescribed form, obtain the requisite signatures, authenticate it with his signature and seal, preserve the original, provide copies to the spouses and forward the prescribed copy to the Union Council. Where the marriage is solemnized by someone other than the Nikah Registrar, that person must complete the prescribed form and deliver it, along with the registration fee, to the concerned Nikah Registrar, who must thereafter process it in the same manner as a marriage solemnized by him. The statutory scheme also imposes liability for non-compliance, including penalties for failure to report a marriage or violation of the conditions of the licence. Thus, the role of the Nikah Registrar is essentially public and statutory: to ensure that the marriage is properly documented, authenticated, preserved and incorporated into the official record. His functions assume particular importance because the Nikahnama records the terms and conditions agreed between the spouses and serves as the primary statutory record of their marriage. 36. The issue concerning the dower related columns of the Nikahnama has repeatedly engaged the attention of this Court in cases of Mst. Fakhra Jabeen67, Haseen Ullah68, and Muhammad Yousaf69. 37. In cases of Mst. Fakhra Jabeen, Haseen Ullah and Muhammad Yousaf the court emphasis was that Columns 13 to 16 of the Nikahnama must be read in the light of the parties’ actual intention, rather than mechanically by reference to the headings of the columns. The court further observed that column 13 ordinarily records the cash component of dower, while Column 16 concerns dower in the form of property and may represent the whole or a portion of the dower in addition to cash. Thus, an entry in Column 13 is not, by itself, a rider or substitute for the property recorded in Column 16; where the intention is to provide both, both constitute enforceable components of dower. In case of ambiguity, the Nikahnama must be construed as a whole, with the court primarily seeking to ascertain the parties’ free and informed intention. With utmost respect, I find it difficult to agree with an approach which gives overriding importance to the intention of the parties while treating the particular columns of the Nikahnama as merely incidental. The Nikahnama is not an ordinary private document; it is a statutory form prescribed under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 and the Rules made thereunder. The columns are provided for a purpose, and therefore their language and placement cannot, in my respectful view, simply be brushed aside. In my view, the intention of the parties must certainly be given effect, but that intention should ordinarily be gathered from the Nikahnama itself, read as a whole, and by giving meaning to each of its relevant entries. If the parties have recorded different aspects of dower in different columns, the Court should be slow to disregard that statutory arrangement merely on the assumption that the parties or the Nikah Registrar may not have appreciated the legal significance of those columns. The prescribed form 67 Mst. Fakhra Jabeen and others v. Wasif Ali and others PLD 2026 Supreme Court 20 68 Haseen Ullah v. Mst. Naheed Begum and others PLD 2022 Supreme Court 686 69 Muhammad Yousaf v. Huma Saeed 2024 SCMR 1078 must retain its meaning and purpose. I would, therefore, respectfully take a different view from an approach which makes the perceived intention of the parties the sole or predominant test. Intention is important, but it must be objectively gathered from the document as a whole, including the language, structure and placement of its entries, rather than reconstructed afterwards from oral assertions or circumstances extraneous to the Nikahnama. This, in my respectful opinion, gives proper effect both to the agreement of the spouses and to the statutory character of the Nikahnama. 38. In order to ensure compliance with the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 and the Rules framed thereunder, and to ensure that the terms of Nikah are accurately and unambiguously recorded, the following directions are hereby issued for future compliance: • Nikah Registrars shall strictly use the prescribed Nikahnama and shall ensure that all its relevant columns are properly and carefully completed. No column should be left blank or treated as unnecessary without a lawful basis, as each column has been provided for a specific purpose. • Particular care shall be taken while recording the terms of dower in Columns 13 to 16. The Registrar shall ensure that these columns are completed in a manner that clearly reflects the agreement actually reached between the parties. • Column 13 shall clearly state the total dower agreed between the parties, whether the dower consists of money, movable property or immovable property. • Where any property is agreed to be given as dower, Column 16 shall contain sufficient particulars to identify that property, including its description, measurements, location and the value, if, agreed between the parties. • The Registrar shall read out or explain the relevant entries to the parties before obtaining their signatures/thumbmark particularly where the Nikahnama contains entries relating to dower, special conditions, delegated right of Talaq or any property given as dower. The object should be to ensure that the document reflects the parties' actual agreement. • Any special condition recorded in Column 17 shall be expressed. The Registrar shall record the condition as agreed by the parties and should not introduce terms of his own. • The Registrar shall not make any entry on the basis of assumption or personal understanding. Where the parties' agreement is unclear, he should seek clarification from the parties before completing the relevant column. • After completion and execution of the Nikahnama, the Registrar shall properly authenticate and preserve the record, provide the prescribed copies to the spouses and forward the requisite copy to the concerned Union Council in accordance with law. • The competent authorities, particularly the Chairman/Secretary concerned Union Councils, shall ensure that all licensed Nikah Registrars are adequately familiar with the statutory purpose and proper manner of completing each column of the prescribed Nikahnama, with particular attention to Columns 13 to 16. • Periodic training or orientation of Nikah Registrars shall be arranged so that the prescribed form is not filled mechanically and the terms agreed between the parties are accurately reflected. • The competent authorities, particularly the Secretary shall periodically inspect the registers maintained by Nikah Registrars to ensure compliance with the Ordinance, the Rules and the conditions of their licences. • Where a Nikah Registrar fails to perform his statutory duties or violates the conditions of his licence, the competent authority should take action in accordance with law.
